newsitem.title: MEXICO: Top Mexico lawmaker says warning flashing on peso.
newsitem.headline: Top Mexico lawmaker says warning flashing on peso.

text.p: The head of the influential Finance Committee in Mexico's Congress said on Tuesday a yellow warning light was flashing over the peso, which is appreciating in real terms against the dollar.

"I think it's important that public opinion and Congress draw attention in time to a sign that was not drawn attention to in 1994," Francisco Suarez Davila, ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) Congressman, said in a Reuters interview.
"And that sign is that a yellow warning light is flashing, and ...is saying that the exchange rate is appreciating."

He said the peso, which he described as solid at present, had gained some 15 percent in real terms against the dollar this year, chiefly because of inflows of short-term capital that he noted were reversible.
"We've already seen it (during the 1994 peso devaluation) and there comes a moment when people begin to worry," he said.

Suarez Davila, who oversees the budget in Congress and whose committee also monitors Banco de Mexico, suggested Mexico adopt a system as in Chile, where the exchange rate is monitored in real terms. He suggested Mexico's central bank should buy reserves and let the peso slide against the dollar.

"Either the price of the peso rises against the dollar, or you leave the price and what goes up is the amount of dollars, (and international) reserves," he said, indicating the central bank should take the latter course.

He also pointed to a debate between Banco de Mexico and other members of the financial community over whether the peso should be used as an anchor for controlling inflation, or a means of ensuring a healthy balance of payments.

"The exchange rate should serve more to maintain a strong, competitive balance of payments," he said, though he acknowledged that at times recently a strong peso has helped Banco de Mexico curb inflation.

He said the concerns on the peso would be raised to Banco de Mexico officials soon when they meet with the Congressional Finance Committee to discuss the central bank's first half financial statement.
